{{Short description|Ornamental pattern in works of art}}
{{See also|Flower of Life (geometry)|Overlapping circles grid#Hexagonal}}
[[File:Hexafoil (fixed width).svg|thumb|A geometrical hexafoil]]

The '''hexafoil''' is a design with six-fold [[dihedral group|dihedral symmetry]] composed from six ''[[vesica piscis]]'' lenses arranged radially around a central point, often shown enclosed in a circumference of another six lenses. It is also sometimes known as a "daisy wheel".<ref name="easton"/> A second, quite different, design is also sometimes referred to by this name; see [[#Alternate symbol|alternate symbol]].

The design is found as a [[rosette (design)|rosette]] ornament in artwork dating back to at least the [[Late Bronze Age]].<ref name=Hoyrup>{{cite journal |last=Høyrup |first=J. |year=2000 |title=Geometrical Patterns in the Pre-classical Greek Area. Prospecting the Borderland between Decoration, Art, and Structural Inquiry |journal=Revue d'histoire des mathématiques |volume=6 |number=1 |pages=5–58 |url=http://www.numdam.org/article/RHM_2000__6_1_5_0.pdf}}</ref>

==Construction==
[[File:Flower of life 6-levels.svg|thumb|The seven overlapping circles grid forms a [[triangular lattice]], seen here with hexagonal rings of [[centered hexagonal number|1, 7, 19, 37, 61 and 91]] circles.<ref>[http://www.metmuseum.org/learn/for-educators/publications-for-educators/islamic-art-and-geometric-design Islamic Art and Geometric Design: Activities for Learning ]</ref>]]
The pattern figure can be drawn by [[pen]] and [[compass (drafting)|compass]], by creating seven interlinking circles of the same diameter touching the previous circle's center. The second circle is centered at any point on the first circle. All following circles are centered on the intersection of two other circles.

[[File:Flower-construction.svg|500px|]]

The design is sometimes expanded into a regular [[overlapping circles grid]]. Bartfeld (2005) describes the construction: "This design consists of circles having a 1-[inch] radius, with each point of intersection serving as a new center. The design can be expanded ''ad infinitum'' depending upon the number of times the odd-numbered points are marked off."<ref name="HTCSGM">{{cite book |title=How to Create Sacred Geometry Mandalas |last=Bartfeld |first=Martha |location=Santa Fe, NM |publisher=Mandalart Creations |date=2005 |page=35}}, citing Drunvalo Melchizedek, ''The Ancient Secret of the Flower of Life'' (1999). The attribution of the term "Flower of Life" to Melchizedek (1999) is also found in {{citation |title=A New Kind of Science |author=Wolfram, Stephen |year=2002 |publisher=[[Wolfram Research |Wolfram Media, Inc.]] |publication-date=May 14, 2002 |isbn=1-57955-008-8 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/newkindofscience00wolf/page/43 43 and 873–874] |url=https://archive.org/details/newkindofscience00wolf/page/43 |url-access=registration}} and in {{citation |title=CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Second Edition |page=1079 |author=Weisstein, Eric W. |date=12 December 2002 |publisher=[[CRC Press]] |publication-date=2002 |isbn=1420035223 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=D_XKBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA1079}}.</ref>

==Usage==
[[File:Estela de Can Peixau.jpg|thumb|Iberian funerary stele of Badalona, Spain (1st century BC)]]
The hexafoil has been very widely used throughout European folk art for a very long period of time. It is attested from at least the beginning of the [[Late Bronze Age]],<ref name=Hoyrup/> represented, for example, on ornamental golden disks found in [[Grave Circle A, Mycenae|Shaft Grave III]] at [[Mycenae]] (16th century BC).<ref>Excavated by [[Heinrich Schliemann]] in 1876. Schliemann, ''Mykenae'' (1878), pp. 165&ndash;172.</ref> It is also found in some [[Cantabrian stelae]], dated to the Iron Age, as well as Norwegian bronze kettles from the same period<ref name="garshol"/>

The six-petal rosette is common in 17th to 20th century [[folk art]] throughout Europe.

In [[Portugal]], it is common to find it in medieval churches and cathedrals, as the engraved signature of a mason; but also as decoration and symbol of protection on the chimneys of old houses in [[Alentejo]] (at times together with the [[lauburu]], or with the [[pentagram]]).

In [[Galicia (Spain)]] and all the [[Cantabrian Mountains]], hexafoils are found since the Iron Age in torc terminals and decoration, and is still used in folk art.<ref>{{cite book |publisher=Baía Edicións |isbn=978-84-9995-329-8 |last=Romero |first=Bieito |title=Simboloxía Máxica en Galicia |location=A Coruña |date=2019 |pages=70–95}}</ref>

It can also be found in the [[Pyrenees]] ([[Navarre]], [[Aragon]], and [[Catalonia]]).<ref>Ariel Golan, ''Prehistoric Religion: Mythology, Symbolism'', (2003), p. 54.</ref> Since 2003 the hexafoil is being used as the logo of the [[Alt Pirineu Natural Park]], the largest of Catalonia.<ref>{{cite book |last=Abella |first=Jordi |title=La integració del patrimoni immaterial en els espais naturals protegits. La sexafòlia a l’alt Pirineu |last2=Garriga |first2=Marc |publisher=Silene |year=2023 |editor-last=Perarnau |editor-first=Xavier |location=Barcelona |pages=26–27 |language=ca |chapter=El cas de logotip del Parc Natural de l’Alt Pirineu |url=https://www.silene.ong/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/La-sexafolia-i-la-integracio-del-patrimoni-immaterial-en-els-espais-naturals-protegits-.pdf}}</ref>

In the [[United Kingdom]] the hexafoil is commonly found on churches, but also in barns and private buildings, as well as on cross slabs.<ref name="garshol"/> The use of the hexafoil as a folk magic symbol was brought from the United Kingdom to [[Australia]] by settlers, where six leaf designs with concentric circles have been found in homes and occasionally in public buildings to serve as a sign of protection.<ref name="2017-02-22_ABC">[http://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-02-21/hexafoil-markings-point-to-hidden-magical-past/8290464 Mysterious hexafoil markings in Australian homes point to hidden magical past], Nicole Dyer, and Damien Larkins, [[ABC News Online]], 2017-02-22</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Evans |first=Ian J |title=Defence Against the Devil: Apotropaic Marks in Australia |language=en |journal=Trust News Australia |date=November 2013 |page=14 |url=https://www.academia.edu/4148179}}</ref>

The hexafoil was also widely used on [[funerary art in Puritan New England|gravestones in Colonial America]], especially popular in parts of Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania. The design was commonly used from the later 17th century until the early 19th century.

The design is also known as "[[Sun of the Alps]]" (''Sole delle Alpi'') in [[Italy]] from its widespread use in alpine folk art.<ref>{{cite web |publisher=Lega Nord |title=Il significato del simbolo del Sole delle Alpi |language=it |url=http://www.prov-varese.leganord.org/doc/solealpi.htm |access-date=December 1, 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140112135050/http://www.prov-varese.leganord.org/doc/solealpi.htm |archive-date=January 12, 2014}}</ref> It resembles a pattern often found in that area on buildings.<ref>{{cite web |author=Ivano Dorboló |title=The church of S.Egidio and the Sun of the Alps symbol |date=June 6, 2010 |website=Storia di Confine – Valli di Natisone |url=http://www.matajur.it/Sito%20English/21-S.Egidio/S.Egidio.htm |access-date=November 9, 2015}}</ref> It is used in the coat of arms of [[Lecco Province]]. It has also been used as the emblem of [[Padanian nationalism]] in northern Italy since the 1990s. In 2001, ''Editoriale Nord'', the publishing company of ''La Padania'', registered the green-on-white design as a trademark.<ref>[http://www.uibm.gov.it/uibm/dati/Titolare.aspx?load=info&id=1439175&table=TradeMark Ufficio Italiano Brevetti e Marchi] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140201142644/http://www.uibm.gov.it/uibm/dati/Titolare.aspx?load=info&id=1439175&table=TradeMark |date=2014-02-01}}, registrazione del simbolo del ''Sole delle Alpi''. According to Rosanna Sapori of ''Radio Padania Libera'', the trademark as of August 2010 was owned by [[Silvio Berlusconi]], who would have obtained it in exchange for the bailout of the bankrupt ''Credieuronord'' bank [https://web.archive.org/web/20100828020905/http://www.ilriformista.it/stories/Prima%20pagina/253357/ «Vi racconto perché Bossi è prigioniero di Berlusconi»] ''Il Riformista'' 28 August 2010.</ref>

In [[Norway]] it can mostly be found on wooden objects, such as beer bowls, clothes smoothing boards, milk butts, wooden chests, beds, and so on, but it can also be found on the doors of buildings. In Norwegian it's sometimes known as "Olavsrose" (rose of [[Olaf II of Norway|Olaf]]), although that name is used for another symbol as well.<ref name="garshol">{{cite journal |last=Garshol |first=Lars Marius |date=2021 |title=Olav's Rose, Perun's Mark, Taranis's Wheel |journal=Peregrinations |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=121–151 |url=https://digital.kenyon.edu/perejournal/vol7/iss4/7/}}</ref>

In [[Lithuania]] the hexafoil was found on wooden beer bowls, spindles, and other wooden objects. It is known as "little sun" (saulute) in Lithuanian.<ref name="garshol"/>

In [[Slovakia]], southeastern [[Poland]] and western [[Ukraine]], the mark was commonly carved on roof beams inside peasant huts. In Ukraine it was known as "the symbol of Perun" (''Peruna znak'') and "the thunder mark" (''gromovoi znak'').<ref>{{cite web |author=Areta Kovalska |title=A Protection Symbol for the Home: The Six-Petal Rosette on the Crossbeams of Galicia |date=October 10, 2018 |website=Forgotten Galicia |url=https://forgottengalicia.com/a-protection-symbol-for-the-home-the-six-petal-rosette-on-the-crossbeams-of-galicia/ |access-date=2021-12-27}}</ref>

In the [[Russian North]] the hexafoil was carved near the outside roof of peasant houses to protect them against lightning. The symbol was known as the thunder sign (''gromovoi znak'') or the thunder wheel (''gromovoe koleso''), and was associated with the thunder god [[Perun]].<ref name="ivanits">{{cite book |title=Russian Folk Belief |last=Ivanits |first=Linda J. |publisher=[[M. E. Sharpe]] |year=1989 |page=17}}</ref>

==Origin==

The origin and meaning of the symbol are not known, but many researchers have independently suggested that it is of religious origin,<ref>{{cite book |title=Die Bauernhäuser des Kantons Graubünden |last=Simonett |first=Christoph |publisher=Verlag Schweizerische Gesellschaft für Volkskunde |date=1965 |pages=224–226}}</ref> and very likely served as a protective symbol.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Weiser-Aall |first=Lily |title=Magiske tegn på norske trekar |date=1947 |journal=By og Bygd |volume=5 |pages=127}}</ref><ref name="easton">{{cite book |last=Easton |first=Timothy |date=2016 |editor-last=Hutton |editor-first=Ronald |title=Physical Evidence for Ritual Acts, Sorcery, and Witchcraft in Christian Britain |publisher=Palgrave Historical Studies in Witchcraft and Magic |pages=39–67 |chapter=Apotropaic symbols and other measures for protecting buildings against misfortune |isbn=978-1-137-44482-0}}</ref><ref name="ivanits"/> There are two main theories for its meaning and origin.

===Solar symbol===
Peralta Labrador (1989) cites a proposal according to which the design in the La Tène ([[Celtiberians|Celtic]]) period was a solar symbol associated with the god [[Taranis]].<ref>Eduardo Peralta Labrador, ''Las estelas discoideas de Cantabria'' in: '' Estelas discoideas de la Peninsula Iberica'' (1989), pp 425–466, citing the opinion of José María Blázquez Martínez.</ref> Other researchers have also described it as a solar symbol,<ref>{{cite book |title=Kors i kake, skurd i tre |last=Østmoe Kostveit |first=Åsta |date=1997 |publisher=Landbruksforlaget |language=no |page=58}}</ref><ref name="easton"/> but no reasoning for this has been given. However, the Lithuanian ("little sun") and Italian ("sun of the Alps") names do suggest a solar origin.

===Thunder wheel===
Garshol (2021) suggests that the rosette is actually a wheel with spokes, and that it originally signified the [[Proto-Indo-European]] thunder god [[Perkwunos]], later becoming associated with his various incarnations, such as [[Perun]], [[Tarḫunz]], [[Taranis]], [[Thor]], and [[Jupiter (mythology)|Jupiter]]. The Russian and Ukrainian names of the symbol, as well as other more involved arguments, are given as rationale.<ref name="garshol"/>

==Alternate symbol==
[[File:Italian - Mirror Case with the Gift of the Rose - Walters 71281.jpg|thumb|Ivory mirror case with a hexafoil motif (alternate form)]]

The name '''hexafoil''' is sometimes also used to refer to a different geometric design that is used as a traditional element of [[Gothic architecture]],<ref>{{citation |title=Geometry and the silversmith: the Domcha Collection |last1=Hartop |first1=Christopher |last2=Norton |first2=Jonathan |publisher=[[John Adamson (publisher) |John Adamson]] |year=2008 |isbn=9780952432289 |quotation=The trefoil, quatrefoil, hexafoil, and octofoil, essential elements of Gothic architecture, all figure in medieval silver.}}</ref> created by overlapping six circular arcs to form a [[flower]]-like image.<ref>{{citation |title=Handbook of Technical Terms Used in Architecture and Building and Their Allied Trades and Subjects |last=Passmore |first=Augustine C. |publisher=Scott, Greenwood, and Company |year=1904 |page=178 |quotation=A geometrical figure used in tracery; it is composed of six lobes or parts of circles joining each other. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NawaAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA178}}</ref><ref>{{citation |title=The Britannica encyclopedia of American art: a special educational supplement to the Encyclopædia Britannica |last=Rugoff |first=Milton |quotation=A geometrical figure with six lobes, used as the form of a silver platter or a wooden decorative panel. |publisher=Encyclopædia Britannica Educational Corp. |year=1976 |page=636}}</ref> The hexafoil design is modeled after the six petal [[Lilium|lily]], for its symbolism of purity and relation to the [[Trinity]].<ref name=":2">{{cite book |title=The Civil Engineer and Architect's Journal |last=Laxton |first=William |date=1856 |publisher=Published for the proprietor |language=en |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XPXNAAAAMAAJ&q=hexafoil+in+architecture&pg=PA256}}</ref> The hexafoil form is created from a series of compound units, and exists as a more complex variation of the same extruded figure.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Natural System of Architecture, as Opposed to the Artificial System of the Present Day |last=Griffith |first=William Pettit |author-link=William Pettit Griffith |date=1845 |publisher=Gilbert and Rivington |language=en |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1uZhAAAAcAAJ&q=hexafoil+in+architecture&pg=PA33}}</ref> Other forms similar to the hexafoil include the [[trefoil]], [[quatrefoil]], and cinquefoil.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Chiffriller |first=Joe |title=Tips & Tricks to Gothic Geometry |date=2002 |journal=New York Carver |via=PBworks |url=http://westongeometry.pbworks.com/w/file/fetch/62270876/TIPSTRICKS.pdf}}</ref>

The other hexafoil design is implemented in various Gothic buildings constructed in the 12th through 16th century. The traditional design is used in [[cloister]]s, [[triforium]]s, and [[stained glass]] windows of famous buildings such as [[Notre-Dame de Paris|Notre-Dame]], [[Salisbury Cathedral]], and [[Regensburg Cathedral]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The World's Best Photos of hexafoil - Flickr Hive Mind |website=hiveminer.com |language=en-US |url=https://hiveminer.com/Tags/hexafoil |access-date=2018-11-12 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181112102857/https://hiveminer.com/Tags/hexafoil |archive-date=2018-11-12}}</ref> Stone cut-out hexafoils are displayed in a plate tracery style in the Salisbury Cathedral, creating a pattern along the triforium.<ref>{{cite web |title=Salisbury Cathedral |website=Khan Academy |language=en |url=https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/medieval-world/gothic1/a/salisbury-cathedral |access-date=2018-11-17}}</ref>

It can also be seen as a framing design in ''[[Bible moralisée]]''.<ref name=":0"/> They are often rendered in [[red]], [[blue]], [[gold (color)|gold]], or vibrant [[orange (colour)|orange]] and surround biblical scenes in the bible.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ey3F_rZwNTUC/page/n294 282] |title=The Art of Illumination: The Limbourg Brothers and the Belles Heures of Jean de France, Duc de Berry |last=Husband |first=Timothy B. |date=2008 |publisher=Metropolitan Museum of Art, Yale University Press |isbn=9781588392947 |language=en |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_ey3F_rZwNTUC |quote=hexafoil in architecture.}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=Microfilms and Fascimilies Database // Medieval Institute Library // University of Notre Dame |website=medieval-microfilms-and-facsimiles.library.nd.edu |url=https://medieval-microfilms-and-facsimiles.library.nd.edu/catalog/facsimile-558 |access-date=2018-11-12 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190728165719/https://medieval-microfilms-and-facsimiles.library.nd.edu/catalog/facsimile-558 |archive-date=2019-07-28}}</ref> The hexafoil style of framing was often used in conjunction with architectural framing to provide the text with more depth, creativity, invention, and volume.<ref name=":0"/> [[Old Testament]] illustrations were surrounded by hexafoil frames while [[moralization]] depictions favored architectural frames.<ref name=":1"/>
